{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

tidymodels is too large to run in a browser, so these exercises practise the *ideas* of Chapter 10 with functions that come with R: splitting the data yourself, fitting with `glm()`, and measuring accuracy and AUC. The downloadable project at the bottom uses tidymodels, exactly as in the chapter. Where you see `______`, replace it with your own code.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: [ex1, ex2, ex3, ex4, ex5]
library(dplyr)
library(rpart)
students      <- read.csv("students.csv")
semesters     <- read.csv("semesters.csv")
questionnaire <- read.csv("questionnaire.csv")
scores <- questionnaire |>
  mutate(
    stress_4 = 6 - stress_4,
    stress   = rowMeans(pick(stress_1:stress_6), na.rm = TRUE),
    support  = rowMeans(pick(support_1:support_6), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  select(student_id, stress, support)
dropout_data <- students |>
  left_join(scores, join_by(student_id)) |>
  left_join(semesters |> filter(semester == 1), join_by(student_id)) |>
  mutate(dropout = as.integer(considering_dropout == "Yes")) |>
  select(dropout, stress, support, financial_worry, sleep_hours, study_hours,
         caffeine_mg, wellbeing, gpa) |>
  na.omit()

# The AUC: how often an at-risk student gets a higher predicted probability
# than a student not at risk
auc <- function(prob, truth) {
  r <- rank(prob); n1 <- sum(truth == 1); n0 <- sum(truth == 0)
  (sum(r[truth == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}

set.seed(10)
train_rows <- sample(nrow(dropout_data), round(0.75 * nrow(dropout_data)))
train <- dropout_data[train_rows, ]
test  <- dropout_data[-train_rows, ]
```

## Splitting and fitting

### Exercise 1: Split the data yourself

The setup code has already split the data: 75% of the rows, chosen at random, for training, and the rest for testing. Check the sizes, and the share of students considering dropout in each set.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex1
nrow(train)
nrow(______)
mean(train$dropout)
mean(test$______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex1" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
nrow(train)
nrow(test)
mean(train$dropout)
mean(test$dropout)
```

About 15% in the training set and 13% in the test set. A simple random split does not guarantee the same share in both; tidymodels' `strata` argument does, which is why the chapter uses it.
:::
:::

### Exercise 2: Fit on training, predict on test

Fit a logistic regression of `dropout` on stress, support, and financial worry, using the training data only. Then predict the probability of dropout for the test students.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex2
model <- glm(dropout ~ stress + support + financial_worry, data = ______, family = binomial)
prob <- predict(model, newdata = ______, type = "response")
head(round(prob, 2))
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex2" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
model <- glm(dropout ~ stress + support + financial_worry, data = train, family = binomial)
prob <- predict(model, newdata = test, type = "response")
head(round(prob, 2))
```
:::
:::

## Evaluating

### Exercise 3: Accuracy and the "always No" model

Classify a test student as at risk if their predicted probability is above 0.5. What share are classified correctly? Compare with a "model" that says "No" for everyone.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex3
model <- glm(dropout ~ stress + support + financial_worry, data = train, family = binomial)
prob <- predict(model, newdata = test, type = "response")
mean((prob > 0.5) == test$dropout)   # the model
mean(test$dropout == ______)          # always "No"
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex3" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
mean((prob > 0.5) == test$dropout)
mean(test$dropout == 0)
```

The model is right about 88% of the time, but "always No" is right about 87% of the time without finding a single student at risk. Accuracy barely separates a useful model from a useless one.
:::
:::

### Exercise 4: The AUC

Use the `auc()` function from the setup to calculate the model's AUC on the test data.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex4
model <- glm(dropout ~ stress + support + financial_worry, data = train, family = binomial)
prob <- predict(model, newdata = test, type = "response")
auc(prob, test$______)
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex4" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
auc(prob, test$dropout)
```

About 0.88: the model ranks an at-risk student above a not-at-risk student about 88% of the time. Unlike accuracy, the AUC clearly shows that the model is useful. (With a small test set, the exact value depends on the random split; the chapter's value differs a little.)
:::
:::

## Overfitting

### Exercise 5: A tree that memorises

Grow a decision tree with no limits (`cp = 0` and `minsplit = 2` let it grow until every leaf is pure), then compare its AUC on the training data with its AUC on the test data.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex5
train$y <- factor(train$dropout)
deep_tree <- rpart(y ~ stress + support + financial_worry + sleep_hours + study_hours +
                     caffeine_mg + wellbeing + gpa,
                   data = train, method = "class",
                   control = rpart.control(cp = 0, minsplit = 2, minbucket = 1))
auc(predict(deep_tree, train)[, "1"], train$dropout)   # on the training data
auc(predict(deep_tree, ______)[, "1"], test$dropout)   # on new students
```

::: { .solution exercise="ex5" }
::: { .callout-tip collapse="false"}
## Solution

```r
auc(predict(deep_tree, train)[, "1"], train$dropout)
auc(predict(deep_tree, test)[, "1"], test$dropout)
```

A perfect 1.0 on the training data, and only about 0.6 on new students, barely better than chance. The tree memorised the training students instead of learning a pattern that carries over. This is overfitting, and it is why a model must always be tested on data it has not seen.
:::
:::
